newsitem.title: UAE: FEATURE - Doha meeting to tackle illegal drug trade.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Doha meeting to tackle illegal drug trade.

text.p: A policeman sat beside a shack that serves as Khor Fakkan port's security checkpoint. He motioned to a row of traditional wooden dhows as workers nearby unloaded sacks onto a truck.
"Smugglers come on dhows like those. For four or five months they study the situation and wait for an opportunity," he said.
"Then they start bringing in the drugs. Sometimes they hide them in car parts and they make goats swallow heroin. They come at night, in the morning, in the afternoon. It's a problem."
Authorities in Khor Fakkan, a sleepy UAE town on the Gulf of Oman below jagged mountains, are battling the drug trade.

But smugglers from Iran, Pakistan and Afghanistan sneak their goods past undercover agents and sniffer dogs to ideal customers just a few hours drive away -- mostly teenagers with plenty of time and money, diplomats and police officials say.
The UAE, an oil-rich Gulf Arab state with long coasts, has recently introduced the death penalty for drug dealers.

But a police official said the UAE remains a major drug transit point in the Middle East. "It's a lucrative business and it is very easy to replace drug traffickers here in the UAE. We need preventative measures," said the official.
Sounder strategies for combating the drug trade across the international narcotics circuit will top the agenda on November 9-11 when experts meet in the Qatari capital Doha.

They will include Gulf specialists and Interpol and U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration officials, who will not have to look much further than the Middle East to grasp the magnitude of the task facing authorities worldwide.
In Lebanon there has been a crackdown, with big traffickers, including a member of the outgoing parliament, being jailed.

Together Lebanon and Syria have reduced cannabis cultivation in the Bekaa Valley and virtually eliminated opium cultivation, the U.S. State Department's Bureau for International Narcotics and Law Enforcement Affairs said in a March 1996 report.
But it said "credible reports of Syrian military protection for drug traffickers persisted in 1995 despite official claims to the contrary."

In Jordan, the problem was not serious, the report said. But added that "trafficking from Lebanon and Syria through Jordan to Egypt and the Gulf states is of concern." Jordan, Syria, Lebanon and Egypt cooperate to stem the trafficking, it added.

In Yemen, drug use and trafficking is rising and its porous frontiers make it an attractive transit point, the report said. Government officials say Yemen is a transit point for illicit drug shipments to Saudi Arabia and Oman, it added.
Even Iran and Saudi Arabia -- the region's most conservative countries that hand down the harshest penalties against smugglers and dealers -- are not immune to drug rings.
In the two-week period to October 9 alone, Iranian police killed eight traffickers and seized over three tonnes of drugs.

More than 1,000 people have been executed in drug-related cases since a 1989 law imposing the death penalty for possession of five kg (11 lb) of opium or 30 grammes (just over one ounce) of heroin took effect. Officials say Iran seized 170 tonnes of drugs in the year to March 1996.

The Islamic republic, where officials say there are about half a million drug addicts, remains a key transit route for narcotics smuggled to Europe from Afghanistan and Pakistan -- the "Golden Crescent".

In Saudi Arabia, convicted smugglers and dealers risk public beheading by the sword, but they continue to target lucrative markets there. Last year, the kingdom executed 192 people, mostly convicted drug smugglers from the Indian sub-continent.

Saudi Interior Minister Prince Nayef recently underlined official concerns when he visited the family of a police major who was killed in a shootout between police and a suspected narcotics gang. The meeting was televised.
"We call upon men of letters and thinkers to make people fully aware of the destructive effects of drugs," he said.
The anti-drug drive has spread to the most remote parts of the neighbouring UAE and in the Fujairah emirate police have mounted a widespread crackdown.
At the local police station's special drug unit, photographs of heroin addicts hang near pictures of convicted drug dealers.
One of the dealers could face execution if an appeals court upholds his death sentence and the UAE president ratifies it.
"The death penalty will make drug operations more difficult, but it will not stop the trade," said a Fujairah police officer.
That's why, police officials say, the UAE has also stepped up a public awareness campaign.

The postal authority has issued stamps with the slogans "Say Yes to Life - No to Drugs" to underscore the dangers of drug use. One shows a man's face -- one half looks healthy, the other shows a haunting skull beside a needle and pills.
